heading: PROPHET HĀRŪN (AS)
title: A VOICE FOR TRUTH, A TRUST TO PROTECT
themes: Brotherhood • Gentle Speech • Tawḥīd • Responsibility • Truth • Patient Counsel
scope: 8 CONNECTED STORIES | 12 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 12 SELECTED QUR’ANIC PASSAGES
reviewNote: Editorial working edition • Every Arabic passage, English meaning and Tafsīr explanation requires final muṣḥaf and qualified scholarly review before publication.
introduction: Volume Fourteen continues the ʿIBRAH Junior journey after Prophet Mūsā (AS). This volume focuses specifically on Prophet Hārūn (AS), whom Allah honoured as a Prophet and appointed in support of his brother Mūsā. Because their missions were connected, some events have appeared previously in the Mūsā volume. Here the focus is different: the gift of a trustworthy helper, Hārūn’s shared call to Tawḥīd, his responsibility for the community during Mūsā’s absence, his opposition to false worship, and the importance of checking facts before blaming someone.

The Qur’an provides selected events rather than a full chronological biography of Hārūn. We do not invent his childhood, private family conversations, travels, profession, date of death or detailed life episodes. In the modern fictional thread, Imaan and Akhlaq prepare a “Trust and Truth” exhibition with Mohsin, Mohsina, Sir Zameer, Dadi Jaan, Salaam and Salamah. Its events are contemporary teaching analogies and never presentations of what happened in Prophetic times.

stories.title: The Second Voice
stories.subtitle: A good helper is a gift

blocks.text: At Sheikh Uncle’s Academy, the exhibition committee had a problem. The invitation cards had been written, the tables were labelled, and the children had decided to call their exhibit “Trust and Truth.” Yet nobody wanted to read the opening announcement. Akhlaq could explain the ideas to a friend, but facing a crowded room made his words tumble into each other. Mohsin offered to speak for him. “Then you will not have to do anything,” he said kindly.

Imaan shook her head. “Helping Akhlaq is not the same as replacing him. Maybe we can divide the task.” That afternoon, Dadi Jaan opened Sūrah Maryam 19:53 and explained that Allah gave Mūsā his brother Hārūn as a prophet, out of His mercy. She carefully distinguished this from school teamwork: Hārūn’s Prophethood was an act of Allah, not a reward for speaking well. Mūsā also asked Allah for help from his family, including Hārūn, as Sūrah Ṭā Hā records.

Akhlaq listened. “So needing help does not make someone weak?” “Not at all,” replied Salaam. “A person can recognise a difficulty, ask Allah for guidance, and seek suitable help.” The next day Mohsin helped Akhlaq practise two short sentences. Imaan checked the facts on the display board. Akhlaq eventually read the welcome; his voice still trembled, but the message was clear.

Afterwards Mohsin did not announce that he had saved the day. He congratulated his friend. Akhlaq wrote on the first exhibit card: A HELPER DOES NOT STEAL SOMEONE ELSE’S PLACE. At the bottom he added: FIRST, THANK ALLAH. The first lesson had begun before the exhibition opened.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Accept suitable help without surrendering responsibility.

stories.title: A Request Made With Humility
stories.subtitle: Ask for the right kind of help

blocks.text: The children had been given a heavy box of donated books. Akhlaq tried to lift it alone and nearly lost his grip. “I can do it!” he insisted. Mohsina pointed to the trolley in the corridor. “You could ask for help before something gets damaged.” They carried the books safely to the library, then sat with Sheikh Uncle to discuss the Qur’anic words in which Mūsā asks Allah to appoint for him a helper from his family, Hārūn his brother.

“This is a supplication from a Prophet,” Sheikh Uncle explained. “Do not flatten it into a school teamwork story. But we can learn that asking Allah and seeking rightful assistance are not shameful.” The children compared three statements written on a board: “I do not need anyone,” “Someone else must solve everything,” and “I will do my part and ask for suitable help.” They realised the third response was responsible. During lunch, Imaan noticed a younger pupil struggling to understand the schedule. Instead of answering every question for her, Imaan explained the first step and invited her to try the next.

Later, Akhlaq thanked Mohsina for noticing the trolley, and Mohsina thanked Mohsin for moving the shelves. Nobody needed a medal. Their reward was a safe library corner that everyone could use. Before going home, Dadi asked what had changed. “We stopped pretending that help is embarrassing,” Akhlaq answered.
“And we stopped pretending that helping means taking control.”

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Ask for help respectfully and help without taking over.

The exhibition posters were ready when a disagreement broke out. One team had changed the programme without informing the others. Akhlaq marched towards the organisers, ready to accuse them of deliberately ruining the plan. Imaan stopped him at the doorway. “You may need to say something firm,” she said, “but you do not yet know why the schedule changed.” The group went to Sir Zameer, who asked them to explain the problem in calm, accurate sentences.

During the lesson he recited the meaning of Sūrah Ṭā Hā 20:44: Mūsā and Hārūn were directed to speak gently to Firʿawn. “It was a divine command to those two Prophets in that specific mission,” he explained, “not an instruction for a child to face a dangerous person.” He invited the students to practise a limited everyday application: respectful words when correcting an ordinary mistake. Akhlaq tried again. “We prepared according to the old timetable. Could you help us understand why it changed?” The teacher explained that one room had been closed for repairs.

Nobody had intended to insult the team. The children adjusted the programme and put up a new notice. Mohsin whispered, “Your first speech would have made enemies.” Akhlaq smiled ruefully. “It might also have been wrong.” On the way home Salamah added an important distinction: being gentle does not mean abandoning the truth, and being truthful does not excuse cruelty. If someone threatens or harms a child, the child should leave and find a trustworthy adult, not try to manage danger alone.
Akhlaq rewrote the poster heading: FIRM ABOUT TRUTH. CAREFUL WITH WORDS.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Speak gently and truthfully; get adult help when safety is at stake.

stories.title: A Message Worth Sharing
stories.subtitle: Speak together for what is right

blocks.text: Sheikh Uncle placed two identical envelopes on the table. One contained a complete announcement; the other had several important lines missing. “Which should we send?” he asked. “The complete one,” replied Imaan. “Even a confident voice cannot make missing facts appear.” Sheikh Uncle reminded them that the Qur’an describes Mūsā and Hārūn being sent with Allah’s signs and a clear authority, calling Firʿawn towards the truth.

Their mission was not the product of a school plan; they were Messengers sent by Allah. The children’s modern task was much smaller. They were preparing a notice about the school’s lost-and-found collection. Akhlaq thought the notice would attract more attention if he wrote, “Every lost item has been recovered.” But several items were still missing. Mohsina suggested, “We can say what we have collected and how families can check the records.” Imaan added a contact procedure.

The notice became less dramatic and more trustworthy. When a younger student asked whether his missing lunchbox had appeared, Akhlaq checked the register instead of guessing. He said, “Not yet. We will tell you if it is found.” The boy looked disappointed, but he was not misled. That evening, Salaam asked which was harder: speaking loudly or speaking accurately.

“Accuracy,” admitted Akhlaq. “Because I sometimes want my words to sound more exciting than the truth.” The family placed another exhibit card beside the first: HONEST INFORMATION IS A FORM OF SERVICE.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Truthful information is better than an impressive claim.

stories.title: The Trust While Someone Is Away
stories.subtitle: Responsible leadership and reform

blocks.text: When Sir Zameer went to a meeting, he asked the older pupils to organise the donated-book table under a supervising teacher’s care. A few students immediately began changing the arrangements. Mohsin suggested a competition for the biggest pile of books. Another child wanted to remove all the labels and start over. Imaan reminded them of their assigned responsibility: make books easy for younger readers to find.

They paused and asked what would actually help. Later, Dadi Jaan read the meaning of Qur’an 7:142, in which Mūsā told his brother Hārūn to take his place among the people, work towards what is right, and not follow the path of those who cause corruption. She explained that this was a serious responsibility within the Prophetic history, not an ordinary classroom appointment. Still, their small fictional experience offered a practical question: does being entrusted with work give us permission to seek attention, or a duty to care for others? The children put the books back into sensible groups and checked the labels with the supervising teacher.

Mohsin admitted that his competition would have made the table crowded and confusing. Imaan answered without mocking him. “Your energy is useful. We just needed to point it somewhere better.” At the end of the day, the younger pupils found books quickly. No one had changed the project into a contest.
On the exhibit board, Akhlaq wrote: RESPONSIBILITY MEANS PROTECTING THE PURPOSE OF A TRUST.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: A trust is a responsibility, not a chance to boast.

stories.title: When the Crowd Changes Direction
stories.subtitle: Truth does not depend on popularity

blocks.text: A colourful rumour spread through the academy: one student claimed a mysterious shortcut could guarantee the highest exam marks. Several pupils began repeating the claim before checking it. Mohsina asked where it came from. Nobody knew. Akhlaq was tempted to join the crowd; he did not want to seem slow.

Sir Zameer gathered the students and read the meaning of Sūrah Ṭā Hā 20:90. In the Qur’anic account, Hārūn had warned his people against the calf-worship and called them to the Most Merciful. He did not approve that false worship. The class did not act out the event or make jokes about it. Instead, they considered an entirely separate modern question: what should a learner do when many people follow a claim that is untrue?

Imaan suggested checking the source and asking a reliable adult. Mohsin added that a correction should not humiliate people. The pupils investigated the exam claim. It had no credible basis. They prepared a notice recommending revision, rest, asking questions, and honest effort rather than imaginary guarantees.

One pupil asked, “What if the whole class laughs at us?” Akhlaq answered, “Being popular cannot make a false statement true.” Their teacher praised the verification process rather than choosing winners and losers. The children placed the card TRUTH IS NOT A VOTE beside their exhibit.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Popularity is not proof of truth.

After the school event, an important art folder went missing. A hurried message in the class group suggested that Mohsin had been responsible for securing it. Before anyone asked what happened, several children blamed him. Akhlaq was ready to repeat the accusation, but Imaan remembered their source lessons about checking facts. The supervising teacher explained that the folder had been moved to a locked cupboard after the exhibition; Mohsin had followed the instructions he was given.

At home, Sheikh Uncle discussed Qur’an 20:92–94 and 7:150 with the family. When Mūsā returned and confronted Hārūn about the people’s wrongdoing, Hārūn explained that he had tried to guide them and feared causing a damaging division. These are serious Qur’anic events; the children were not asked to judge the Prophets or recreate their disagreement. Instead, they studied the careful skill of hearing the full account before reaching conclusions in an ordinary school problem. Akhlaq apologised to Mohsin.

“I treated a rumour as evidence,” he admitted. Mohsin forgave him, but also asked him not to repeat unverified accusations. Sir Zameer invited the children to build a simple checklist: What do I know? What do I not know? Who can clarify safely?
The final sign read: BEFORE BLAME, SEEK FACTS. Akhlaq kept a copy in his notebook.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Check facts and hear explanations before blaming others.

The final day of the exhibition arrived. Each group had to choose one lesson that could change everyday conduct. Akhlaq wanted to describe every poster at once; Imaan reminded him that the strongest presentation was a clear one. Dadi Jaan joined the children at the display and asked who Hārūn was. Mohsina answered: a Prophet honoured by Allah, and the brother and helper of Prophet Mūsā.

Mohsin mentioned the instruction to speak gently while presenting the truth. Imaan remembered Hārūn’s warning against false worship and the responsibility he carried while Mūsā was away. Akhlaq added the lesson he had needed most: do not blame a person without learning what really happened. At the closing circle, Salaam asked the children to choose one voluntary action for the coming week. One chose to thank a helper; another chose to correct a rumour; another promised to speak more respectfully at home.

No one was asked to reveal their deepest feelings, and no child received a public faith score. The class made an ordinary chart of helpful actions, not a ranking of spirituality. Before leaving, Dadi Jaan read the Qur’anic greeting of peace upon Mūsā and Hārūn from Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt. “Allah honours His chosen Messengers,” she said. “We honour their accounts by learning faithfully and living responsibly.” The children packed the compass and the family tree together.
Neither became a magical object; both simply reminded them to look towards good guidance. Akhlaq placed the final card on top of the folder: A GOOD VOICE TELLS THE TRUTH, AND A GOOD HEART ACTS ON IT.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Carry guidance into one small voluntary action.

synthesis.text: Hārūn (AS) was chosen as a Prophet by Allah. Allah answered the request for support through Hārūn, and both brothers were sent with His guidance. They were instructed to speak gently while carrying a grave message of truth. In Mūsā’s absence, Hārūn was entrusted with responsibility among the people; the Qur’an records his warning against the calf-worship and later explanation of his conduct. Allah honours Mūsā and Hārūn in Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt. The children should learn these authenticated points without invented biographical details.
Allah’s guidance, not popularity, establishes right and wrong.
A trustworthy helper strengthens a good task without seeking ownership of it.
Praying and seeking appropriate practical assistance are compatible.
Gentleness is not weakness; firmness does not justify humiliation.
Leadership is safeguarding a trust, not enjoying power.
Do not follow falsehood merely because a crowd does.
Fair judgment requires evidence, listening and willingness to correct a mistake.
Sincere learning appears in small, repeated acts of responsibility.

A caregiver can ask: “Who helped you this week?”, “Was there a moment when careful words prevented harm?”, “How can we check a claim before passing it on?”, and “Who is a trusted adult to contact if something feels unsafe?” Participation is voluntary; children can answer with fictional examples rather than disclose personal experiences.
Did I describe their contribution fairly?
Was I both truthful and kind?
Did I complete the agreed task?
What may I practise next week?
FINAL MUḤĀSABAH • Optional and private: Practised / Still learning / Skip. Never rank children by religious worth, distress, disclosure, or declared intention.

Award only neutral completion indicators such as “Source Explorer”, “Careful Listener”, “Fact Checker” and “Helpful Teammate” for completion of safe learning interactions. Disable public leaderboards and moral/spiritual percentages. No prize is attached to a Prophetic title or religious standing.
